title: Holding Glucose Still
endLine: Hold glucose still, and what enters must equal what leaves.

scenes.tts: A beta cell reads glucose by burning it, then releases insulin. Insulin must then act on liver, muscle and fat. So when glucose climbs too high after a glucose drink, what failed? Too little insulin, or insulin that works too weakly?
scenes.narration: A beta cell reads glucose by burning it, then releases insulin. Insulin must then act on liver, muscle and fat. So when glucose climbs too high after a glucose drink, what failed? Too little insulin, or insulin that works too weakly?
scenes.caption: A beta cell reads glucose by burning it, then releases insulin. Insulin must then act on liver, muscle and fat. So when glucose climbs too high after a glucose drink, what failed? Too little insulin, or insulin that works too weakly?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's colour map: YELLOW = glucose, PURPLE = insulin, BLUE = membrane transporters, GREY = cells, organs and outlines, GREEN tick = supported, RED cross = not identified. New in this film: CYAN = the clamp's glucose pump (external glucose added), MAGENTA = glucose the body makes itself (mostly liver), WHITE = disposal (glucose leaving into tissues). Open on the first film's carried rule row, small at top right: 'glucose -> metabolism -> electrical signal -> insulin', with a three-cell GREY islet icon above it. On 'releases insulin', PURPLE insulin dots stream out of the islet icon and the camera pulls back to reveal THIS FILM'S WORLD, kept for the whole film: a wide translucent band with a GREY outline across the middle labelled 'blood', filling about 60% of the frame width, with YELLOW glucose dots drifting inside it; a GREY 'liver' organ above-left with a YELLOW inflow arrow into the blood; a GREY block below labelled 'muscle and fat' with BLUE transporter doors on its top edge and YELLOW dots leaving the blood through them; at the band's right end a vertical gauge labelled 'blood glucose' with a YELLOW fill. On 'act on liver, muscle and fat', PURPLE dots reach the liver (its inflow arrow thins) and the muscle-and-fat block (more BLUE doors move up from inside the block to its top edge). On 'climbs too high', a GREY cup labelled 'glucose drink' at top centre pours YELLOW dots into the blood and the gauge fill rises past a dashed line marked 'too high' (schematic). On the two questions, two large tags appear beside the gauge in turn: 'too little insulin?' (PURPLE, next to fewer, dimmer insulin dots) and 'weak response?' (BLUE, next to fewer BLUE doors at the surface). Both tags stay, unanswered.
Title 'Holding Glucose Still' fades in at the top for 2 s while the two question tags shrink to the right edge. YELLOW dots keep drifting in the blood band; the gauge sits high.

scenes.tts: The usual test is that drink: seventy-five grams of glucose, then blood glucose readings. In a healthy person, glucose peaks near one hundred forty to one hundred sixty milligrams per deciliter. The curve blends three things: absorption, insulin secretion, and insulin action.
scenes.narration: The usual test is that drink: 75 g of glucose, then blood glucose readings. In a healthy person, glucose peaks near 140 to 160 mg/dL. The curve blends three things: absorption, insulin secretion, and insulin action.
scenes.caption: The usual test is that drink: 75 g of glucose, then blood glucose readings. In a healthy person, glucose peaks near 140 to 160 mg/dL. The curve blends three things: absorption, insulin secretion, and insulin action.
scenes.visual: The gauge resets to its fasting level and grows a trace: a plot unfolds to its right (about 40% of frame width) with x axis 'hours', 0 to 2, and y axis 'mg/dL', 80 to 200. As the drink pours YELLOW dots into the blood, a YELLOW curve draws in real time from 90 at time 0 up to a peak inside a shaded band from 140 to 160 partway through (peak timing schematic), then down below 140 (a thin dashed line at 140) by 2 h. Tag on the curve: 'healthy (shape schematic)'. On 'blends three things', three labels light in turn, each on its source in the world: 'absorption' at the gut inflow, 'secretion' at the PURPLE islet icon, 'action' at the BLUE doors and the liver. Three thin arrows from those labels converge on the curve.

scenes.tts: Reduce secretion, and muscle and fat take up less while the liver releases more. Glucose climbs higher. Now hold insulin constant and weaken its action instead. The same directions follow. Type two diabetes combines too little secretion with frequently reduced action.
scenes.narration: Reduce secretion, and muscle and fat take up less while the liver releases more. Glucose climbs higher. Now hold insulin constant and weaken its action instead. The same directions follow. Type 2 diabetes combines too little secretion with frequently reduced action.
scenes.caption: Reduce secretion, and muscle and fat take up less while the liver releases more. Glucose climbs higher. Now hold insulin constant and weaken its action instead. The same directions follow. Type 2 diabetes combines too little secretion with frequently reduced action.
scenes.visual: Two runs of the same world, one after the other. Run 1, on 'Reduce secretion': PURPLE insulin dots from the islet icon thin out; fewer BLUE doors sit at the surface and fewer YELLOW dots leave; the liver's YELLOW inflow arrow thickens. A second curve draws on the plot, rising higher than the healthy one and coming down more slowly, labelled 'less secretion' (schematic, no numbers on it). Run 2, on 'hold insulin constant': PURPLE dots return to full number, but fewer BLUE doors move to the surface and the liver's inflow arrow stays thick despite the insulin. A dashed curve draws over the 'less secretion' curve along a similar high path (schematic, not claimed identical), labelled 'weaker action'. On 'same directions', both curves pulse together. On 'Type 2 diabetes', a small tag 'type 2: often both' appears beside the two curves.

scenes.tts: Both faults tip one balance. Blood glucose holds steady only while glucose entering the blood equals glucose leaving it. Here, entry runs ahead of exit, so the level climbs. A curve shows that tipping, but not which fault caused it.
scenes.narration: Both faults tip one balance. Blood glucose holds steady only while glucose entering the blood equals glucose leaving it. Here, entry runs ahead of exit, so the level climbs. A curve shows that tipping, but not which fault caused it.
scenes.caption: Both faults tip one balance. Blood glucose holds steady only while glucose entering the blood equals glucose leaving it. Here, entry runs ahead of exit, so the level climbs. A curve shows that tipping, but not which fault caused it.
scenes.visual: The plot shrinks to a small inset at top right. In the world, all entry arrows (gut, liver) gather into one big YELLOW arrow on the left of the blood band labelled 'in', and all exit through the BLUE doors gathers into one big YELLOW arrow on the right labelled 'out'. On 'equals glucose leaving it', the two arrows match in width and the gauge holds still: label above the band, large white text, 'in = out: level holds'. On 'entry runs ahead', the 'in' arrow widens, the 'out' arrow stays narrow, and the gauge fill climbs. On 'not which fault', the two question tags from the hook ('too little insulin?', 'weak response?') return beside the inset curve, each with a question mark; neither is chosen.

scenes.tts: So hold glucose still on purpose. A hyperglycemic clamp holds glucose high and watches the insulin response: the beta cell's side. A second clamp asks about action. It holds insulin at a raised plateau. A pump adds glucose, adjusted by repeated measurements, to keep glucose near basal.
scenes.narration: So hold glucose still on purpose. A hyperglycemic clamp holds glucose high and watches the insulin response: the beta cell's side. A second clamp asks about action. It holds insulin at a raised plateau. A pump adds glucose, adjusted by repeated measurements, to keep glucose near basal.
scenes.caption: So hold glucose still on purpose. A hyperglycemic clamp holds glucose high and watches the insulin response: the beta cell's side. A second clamp asks about action. It holds insulin at a raised plateau. A pump adds glucose, adjusted by repeated measurements, to keep glucose near basal.
scenes.visual: The drink cup fades out for good (no gut entry from here on). On 'hold glucose still', a horizontal clamp bracket snaps onto the gauge, pinning its fill; label 'held'. On 'hyperglycemic clamp', the pinned level is set high, and PURPLE insulin dots stream from the islet icon; a tag 'beta cell's side' appears by the islet. On 'A second clamp', the small inset plot and the islet icon fade out, and the gauge's pinned level slides down to a mark labelled 'basal', and the islet tag fades. On 'raised plateau', a PURPLE insulin gauge appears at left, its fill rising to a flat high line labelled 'insulin: raised plateau'; PURPLE dots now bathe the liver and the muscle-and-fat block, and many BLUE doors move up to the surface. On 'A pump adds glucose', a CYAN pump with a line into the blood band appears at top left and pushes CYAN-outlined YELLOW dots in. On 'repeated measurements', a small CYAN loop arrow runs from the gauge back to the pump, and the pump's rate dial twitches up and down while the gauge stays pinned at basal. Label on the pump: 'pump'.

scenes.tts: Glucose is not changing, so glucose in equals glucose out. Disposal, the glucose leaving into tissues, equals the pump rate plus glucose the body still makes. That inner source is mostly the liver. This holds when almost no glucose is lost in urine.
scenes.narration: Glucose is not changing, so glucose in equals glucose out. Disposal, the glucose leaving into tissues, equals the pump rate plus glucose the body still makes. That inner source is mostly the liver. This holds when almost no glucose is lost in urine.
scenes.caption: Glucose is not changing, so glucose in equals glucose out. Disposal, the glucose leaving into tissues, equals the pump rate plus glucose the body still makes. That inner source is mostly the liver. This holds when almost no glucose is lost in urine.
scenes.visual: Show, then tell: the flows in the world become bars. A CYAN bar grows from the pump's line, labelled 'pump (J)'; a smaller MAGENTA bar grows from the liver's inflow, labelled 'body makes (EGP)'; they stack, and beside them a WHITE bar grows from the blood band's lower edge (all glucose leaving, not only through the BLUE doors), labelled 'disposal (Rd): all tissues', reaching exactly the same height as the stack. Bar heights schematic here. On 'in equals glucose out', a large '=' appears between the stack and the WHITE bar. The equation fades in above, large: 'Rd = J + EGP'. On 'mostly the liver', the MAGENTA bar and the liver pulse together. On 'lost in urine', a small tag appears under the equation: 'urine loss negligible'.

scenes.tts: Two healthy adults, same raised insulin, same steady glucose. Suppose the liver adds nothing. A's pump runs at five point seven one milligrams per kilogram per minute. B's runs at two point eight six. Whose tissues answer insulin more weakly?
scenes.narration: Two healthy adults, same raised insulin, same steady glucose. Suppose the liver adds nothing. A's pump runs at 5.71 mg per kg per min. B's runs at 2.86. Whose tissues answer insulin more weakly?
scenes.caption: Two healthy adults, same raised insulin, same steady glucose. Suppose the liver adds nothing. A's pump runs at 5.71 mg per kg per min. B's runs at 2.86. Whose tissues answer insulin more weakly?
scenes.visual: The world splits into two simplified copies side by side, 'A' and 'B'; each keeps only its blood band with the glucose gauge pinned at basal, a small PURPLE tag 'same insulin', its liver and its CYAN pump. On 'the liver adds nothing', both MAGENTA bars shrink to zero and a tag 'liver: 0 (assumed)' appears under each liver. On the pump rates, each CYAN pump bar grows to scale on a shared axis 'mg per kg per min', 0 to 7: A to 5.71, B to 2.86 (both numbers on screen; values are the lesson's made-up worked example; tag 'made-up data'). Question card across the top in white: 'Whose tissues respond less?' The WHITE disposal bars are NOT yet drawn.

Predict pause. The question card stays. Both CYAN pumps keep pushing dots in at their rates (B visibly slower); both glucose gauges stay pinned at basal; PURPLE insulin gauges flat and equal. No other change.

scenes.tts: B's. With nothing else entering, the pump rate is disposal. B removes about half as much glucose at the same insulin. That shows lower insulin-stimulated disposal, but not which step inside the cells is weaker.
scenes.narration: B's. With nothing else entering, the pump rate is disposal. B removes about half as much glucose at the same insulin. That shows lower insulin-stimulated disposal, but not which step inside the cells is weaker.
scenes.caption: B's. With nothing else entering, the pump rate is disposal. B removes about half as much glucose at the same insulin. That shows lower insulin-stimulated disposal, but not which step inside the cells is weaker.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. In each copy a WHITE disposal bar grows beside the CYAN bar to the same height: A 5.71, B 2.86. On 'about half', a bracket compares them: '2.86 / 5.71 = 0.50' and label 'about half'. In B, fewer YELLOW dots leave through the BLUE doors than in A. On 'not which step', a zoom-in circle on B's muscle-and-fat block shows a GREY cell outline with a large RED question mark inside and a small RED cross labelled 'defect not identified'.

scenes.tts: But insulin cuts the liver's output and may not stop it. So that output is estimated with a tracer, distinguishably labeled glucose. Then disposal is the pump plus the liver's share, measured, not assumed.
scenes.narration: But insulin cuts the liver's output and may not stop it. So that output is estimated with a tracer, distinguishably labeled glucose. Then disposal is the pump plus the liver's share, measured, not assumed.
scenes.caption: But insulin cuts the liver's output and may not stop it. So that output is estimated with a tracer, distinguishably labeled glucose. Then disposal is the pump plus the liver's share, measured, not assumed.
scenes.visual: Copy B fades; copy A slides back to the centre as the single world. The tag 'liver: 0 (assumed)' gets a RED cross. On 'may not stop it', a thin MAGENTA trickle of dots leaves the liver into the blood. On 'tracer', a few YELLOW dots with bright MAGENTA rings (labelled 'tracer') enter from the pump, mix in the blood, and a small counter on the blood band, labelled 'blood samples', reads out the MAGENTA bar: it grows to 0.50 on the same axis. On 'pump plus the liver's share', the MAGENTA 0.50 stacks on A's CYAN 5.71, and the WHITE disposal bar grows to match: 6.21 (computed: 5.71 + 0.50, the lesson's worked example). Tag 'measured, not assumed' with a GREEN tick.

scenes.tts: So a glucose curve shows the balance tipping, not why. Freeze the level, and the balance turns into a measurement. What the pump adds, plus what the body makes, is what the tissues take.
scenes.narration: So a glucose curve shows the balance tipping, not why. Freeze the level, and the balance turns into a measurement. What the pump adds, plus what the body makes, is what the tissues take.
scenes.caption: So a glucose curve shows the balance tipping, not why. Freeze the level, and the balance turns into a measurement. What the pump adds, plus what the body makes, is what the tissues take.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the full world from the opening. On 'tipping, not why', the small inset curve and the two hook tags glow briefly beside the gauge. On 'Freeze the level', the clamp bracket pins the gauge and the 'in' and 'out' arrows settle to equal width. On 'What the pump adds', the CYAN pump pulses; on 'what the body makes', the liver's MAGENTA trickle pulses; on 'what the tissues take', the YELLOW dots leaving through the BLUE doors pulse. The 'Rd = J + EGP' equation sits large above the band.

End card over the dimmed but still moving world (CYAN and MAGENTA glucose entering, YELLOW dots leaving through the BLUE doors, gauge pinned). Large white text, centred: 'Hold glucose still, and what enters must equal what leaves.'
